standards.name: MIxS (Minimum Information about any (X) Sequence)
standards.abstract: MIxS is a community-developed metadata specification for nucleotide sequence records and their contextual (sampling and experimental) metadata. It targets genomic, metagenomic, marker-gene and related sequence data, describing samples collected from natural, host-associated or engineered environments and the methods used to obtain and process nucleic acids and sequencing. The standard is maintained by the Genomic Standards Consortium (GSC) and provides modular checklists (technology-specific “checklists”) and environment-specific “extensions” (formerly packages) to ensure a minimal, consistent set of metadata accompanies sequence submissions. MIxS addresses the problem of sparse and heterogeneous contextual annotation of sequence records by defining named terms, expected value syntaxes, occurrence rules and recommended ontologies, distributed as downloadable spreadsheets and machine-readable LinkML/YAML artifacts.

classification.rationale: The source material presents MIxS as explicit, named metadata terms arranged in checklists and spreadsheet columns (structured comment name, item, definition, expected value, value syntax, occurrence, etc.). This is a genuine field-level table of metadata terms (checklists and environmental-package subtables) rather than only narrative guidance, so it should be modelled as a MetadataTable.

standards.name: MIGS (Minimal Information about a Genome Sequence)
standards.abstract: MIGS defines a checklist of metadata fields for genome and nucleic-acid sequence reports. It covers descriptions of the investigation and project, sampling/collection (geographic location, date, environmental descriptors), and properties of the nucleic acid/genome (replicon counts, estimated size, ploidy, lineage), plus environment-specific subpackages (air, soil, host-associated, etc.). The standard is produced and maintained by the Genomic Standards Consortium (GSC) to make genomic data discoverable and interoperable by providing a machine-readable minimal metadata checklist (MIGS/MIMS/MIENS) with explicit value syntax and links to ontologies.

classification.rationale: Source materials are published as structured checklists / spreadsheet sheets that list named fields with definitions and explicit value syntax (e.g. 'structured comment name', 'Value syntax', examples). The source therefore presents genuine field-level structure (a metadata table) rather than only prose guidance.

standards.name: MIMS (Minimum Information about a Metagenome Sequence)
standards.abstract: MIMS targets metagenomic sequencing projects: it specifies the minimal metadata to describe a metagenome sequence so that datasets (sequence reads and assembled data) and their contextual information are discoverable, interpretable and reusable. The seed material is a Genomic Standards Consortium (GSC) workshop page describing the development and community activities around MIMS/MIGS: it documents workshop sessions on checklist/schema development, object modeling (FuGE), controlled vocabularies and ontology requirements, and infrastructure topics such as identifiers and data exchange. The standard is maintained by the Genomic Standards Consortium and addresses the problem of incomplete or inconsistent metadata for genomes and metagenomes by promoting community-driven minimum metadata checklists, controlled vocabularies, and implementation pathways (schemas, object models, and informatics integration).

classification.rationale: The source material is prose describing workshop activities, goals, and high-level requirements for MIMS (e.g., sessions on checklist development, semantics, and infrastructure). It does not present a field-level table or a clearly ordered procedural DAG; instead it describes recommended reporting practices and community aims, so its structure is best represented as principles.

principles.principle: Define and promote a "Minimum Information" checklist for metagenome sequences (MIMS).
principles.evidence: "The need for MIMS (“Minimum Information about a Megagenomic Sequence”) and its origins."

principles.principle: Actively develop and maintain a checklist and schema for MIMS to enable implementation by data resources.
principles.evidence: "MIGS/MIMS Technical Session - Active work on next version of checklist and schema with a view to implementation by CAMERA"

principles.principle: Ensure contributors increase the quality and quantity of metadata so that interpretation and analyses can be comprehensive and unhindered, particularly from ecological and environmental perspectives.
principles.evidence: "The primary aim of developing a new standard is to ensure that those researchers generating genomes and metagenomic contribute to an increase in the quality and quantity of metadata, so that interpretation and analyses of the genome collection can be carried out in a comprehensive and unhindered manner, especially from an ecological and environmental perspective."

principles.principle: Standardize descriptions and support exchange and integration of genomic and metagenomic data across resources.
principles.evidence: "the goal of this international community is to promote mechanisms for standardizing the description of genomes and the exchange and integration of genomic data."

principles.principle: Design an explicit object model for MIGS/MIMS implementations (example: based on FuGE).
principles.evidence: "Towards a MIGS/MIMS Object Model based on FuGE."

principles.principle: Use controlled vocabularies and ontologies to support compliant, interoperable metadata records.
principles.evidence: "Controlled vocabulary and Ontology Requirements of GCat: Supporting the completion of compliant MIGS/MIMS reports."

principles.principle: Explore automated/text-mining approaches to help extract metadata from the literature for compliance with MIMS.
principles.evidence: "Text mining options for MIGS/MIMS compliance: Extracting genomic metadata from the literature."

principles.principle: Work toward global identifier mapping and permanent unique identifiers to link genomes and metagenomes across resources.
principles.evidence: "Towards a single, global list of genomes and metagenomes" and "Permanent, unique identifiers in the straininfo.net portal."

principles.principle: Develop the standard through community governance, workshops, and open membership activities led by the Genomic Standards Consortium.
principles.evidence: "The Genomic Standards Consortium (GSC) is an open-membership working body formed in September 2005. The aim of the GSC is making genomic data discoverable."

standards.notes: Extraction based on a GSC workshop page describing MIMS/MIGS activities; the page contains meeting agenda items and session titles rather than a formal checklist table or schema text. Where session titles imply requirements (e.g., controlled vocabularies, object models), those have been captured as principles with verbatim session-title quotes as evidence.

standards.name: MIMARKS (Minimal Information about a Marker Sequence)
standards.abstract: MIMARKS specifies minimal metadata fields to accompany marker sequence data (e.g., 16S rRNA surveys and other targeted amplicon studies) collected from environmental or cultured samples. The standard is maintained as part of the Genomic Standards Consortium/MIGS/MIMS family and is provided as a worksheet-style checklist for submission to INSDC repositories (GenBank/ENA/DDBJ). It addresses what metadata to record (sample geographic location, collection date, investigation type, project, experimental factors, environmental package parameters, value syntax and units) to ensure consistent, machine-readable reporting and to support downstream integration and archive submission.

classification.rationale: The source is a spreadsheet/checklist that lists named metadata items (structured comment name / item) with concrete value syntax, examples, expected values, occurrence and position columns — i.e. a field-level metadata table rather than prose guidance or a process DAG.

standards.name: MIxS Ancient (palaeogenomics) Extension
standards.abstract: This proposal addresses metadata for ancient DNA (aDNA) and palaeogenomics research, where sequencing is performed on destructive, often unique ancient biological and cultural samples and the primary data take the form of DNA sequencing reads and associated metadata. The document is a project proposal maintained within the Genomic Standards Consortium (GSC) to extend existing MIxS checklists so they are compatible with the particular requirements of aDNA. It describes the problem (inconsistent and fragmentary metadata that reduces data discoverability and reuse), the intended solution (a new ‘ancient’ MIxS extension adding descriptors and clarifications, plus submission combinations of minimum essential metadata), community and repository engagement (aiming for ENA/SRA-compatible submission combinations), and ambitions for cross-disciplinary reuse and ethical stewardship of irreplaceable samples.

classification.rationale: Source material is a prose project proposal describing objectives, scope, and planned actions (what to do and why) rather than a field-level metadata table or a sequential workflow. The source contains guidance and plans (instructions/purposes) rather than a concrete table of named fields with data types or a DAG of ordered steps, so it should be classified as 'principle'.

principles.principle: Extend existing MIxS standards for compatibility with ancient DNA.
principles.evidence: "This project extends existing MIxS standards for compatibility with the particular requirements of aDNA."

principles.principle: Generate a new ‘ancient’ extension that adds new metadata descriptors capturing context specific to ancient samples.
principles.evidence: "This will involve generating a new ‘ancient’ extension that adds new metadata descriptors to include crucial context specific for ancient samples, ..."

principles.principle: Extend and clarify definitions of existing MIxS descriptors to ensure compatibility with ancient samples.
principles.evidence: "... extending and clarifying definitions of existing MIxS descriptors to ensure they are compatible with these types of samples."

principles.principle: Develop community-agreed minimum essential metadata submission combinations for different aDNA sub-fields to upload alongside sequence data.
principles.evidence: "The third phase of the project will include a community-agreed standard set of minimum essential metadata for different ancient DNA sub-fields in the form of submission combinations, that should be uploaded alongside sequence data, to ensure consistency across the field and to make it easier for all parties to both upload and download aDNA data."

principles.principle: Improve metadata reporting at the point of data submission (at the source) to public archives such as ENA/SRA.
principles.evidence: "This project aims to improve metadata reporting at ‘the source’ (i.e., at data upload to ENA/SRA databases) to make maintenance of the above databases easier."

principles.principle: Identify and prioritize common descriptors that apply across multiple aDNA sub-disciplines to reduce redundant specialist databases and increase interoperability.
principles.evidence: "By identifying common-descriptors that can apply across multiple aDNA research sub-disciplines, this will help to replace or reduce the necessity for the partly redundant efforts in such specialist databases as described above, as this information would be stored with data on upload."

principles.principle: Develop sub-discipline specific extensions after defining cross-discipline common descriptors.
principles.evidence: "Once these common descriptors are defined, we will develop more sub-discipline specific extensions to account for sub-discipline specific required information."

principles.principle: Design the schema to be reusable as a template for other biomolecular disciplines in archaeological science.
principles.evidence: "We also aim for this schema to be used as a template for other biomolecular disciplines in archaeological science, given the often highly interdisciplinary nature of these fields."

principles.principle: Address ethical and scientific imperatives by ensuring proper curation of metadata for irreplaceable ancient samples.
principles.evidence: "Achieving these goals is an absolute imperative for both the scientific and ethical advancement of the field of ancient DNA. Without proper curation of our past, we neither understand our present nor shape our future."},{

Source material is a project proposal and implementation plan; it does not contain a concrete metadata table of named fields with types or a stepwise DAG, so principles/extracted objectives are presented with verbatim supporting quotes.
